analysis.one_liner: Removes all campaign contribution limits and ends public presidential financing, while requiring faster online disclosure of campaign money.
analysis.headline: Despite 69 cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote in either committee and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would lift every legal limit on how much anyone can give to federal candidates and parties starting in 1999, and would shut down the taxpayer check-off that helps pay for presidential campaigns. It would also require political committees to file reports electronically, report contributions received in the final 90 days of a campaign within 24 hours, and post those reports on the Internet within a day. It also would have required political parties to disclose transfers of unregulated 'soft money' between national and state party committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy donors and large contributors, who could give unlimited sums directly to candidates and parties once limits lapse after 1998, and national and state political parties, which would raise and move far more money. Voters also gain something: faster, searchable online disclosure of who is giving, including 24-hour notice of contributions in the final 90 days of a campaign.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the limits on federal campaign contributions for calendar years beginning after 1998, so donors could give unlimited amounts to candidates and parties.

It requires national party committees to disclose all funds transferred to state or local party committees, regardless of how the money is classified, and requires state and local party committees to copy the FEC on reports they file under state law.

It requires electronic filing of campaign reports, 24-hour reporting of any contribution received in the 90 days before an election, and posting of the reports on the Internet within 24 hours of the FEC receiving them.

It ends the income tax check-off for the Presidential Election Campaign Fund and terminates the fund and the primary matching payment account after 1998, with leftover money transferred to the Treasury's general fund.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary voters without large checks to write: with limits gone, the voices of big donors would count for far more in federal elections, and the voluntary public financing option for presidential campaigns would disappear. Small donors and candidates who rely on many small contributions would compete against unlimited money.

drawbacks.text: The bill's central change is removing all contribution limits, which would let a single wealthy donor give unlimited sums directly to federal candidates and party committees, magnifying the influence of large checks over ordinary voters' voices.
It terminates taxpayer-financed presidential campaigns after 1998, removing the voluntary public financing system that reduced candidates' dependence on private money.

The disclosure improvements are real but partial: they cover party soft-money transfers and late contributions, while the bill simultaneously increases the amount of money flowing into campaigns, so more money would be disclosed but also raised.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency provisions — electronic filing, 24-hour reporting of late contributions, and posting reports online — were genuinely useful and later became standard. But the bill's headline change, unlimited contributions, outweighs them for ordinary voters: it would have let wealthy donors and parties spend without limit, while ending public presidential financing. Even a supporter would have to acknowledge that the disclosure improvements were paired with a change that made money matter far more, not less.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, neither ever held a hearing or voted on it, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. John Doolittle introduced the bill on March 6, 1997, with 69 cosponsors, 67 of them Republicans and 2 Democrats.
It was referred the same day to the House Oversight Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo won on both sides: existing contribution limits and public presidential financing survived, but the faster online disclosure also never happened. No one gained new rights to give unlimited money, and voters did not get the faster disclosure either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo — old limits, old disclosure

for.name: Rep. Tom DeLay and 11 other original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Oversight Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; no hearing or markup was ever held.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill's provisions terminating taxpayer presidential campaign financing.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken on the bill, but its support was heavily Republican: 67 of its 69 cosponsors were House Republicans, with only 2 Democrats.

industries.industry: Wealthy donors and large campaign contributors
industries.note: Removing all contribution limits after 1998 would let a single donor give unlimited sums to federal candidates and parties. Their gain is precisely a loss of relative influence for voters who give small amounts or none at all.

The bill requires parties to disclose soft-money transfers between national and state committees and to file electronically, cutting into their financial secrecy. But with contribution limits gone, parties could raise unlimited money, a far larger gain than the disclosure costs.

They would face heavier compliance burdens — electronic filing, 24-hour reporting of late contributions, and loss of the 'best efforts' excuse for identifying donors. In exchange, they could accept unlimited contributions.
